extracted.intended_audience: parents and tutors educating young gentlemen / guardians responsible for early upbringing
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on educating a young pupil into a balanced, virtuous, adaptable gentleman — combining philosophy, manners, physical training, languages, and natural style. Emphasises early instruction, practice over pedantry, and humane methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should manifest as continual cheerfulness and serenity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness; her state is like that of things in the regions above the moon, always clear and serene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy should make tranquillity and satisfaction appear outwardly — a graceful confidence, active and joyous carriage, and a serene countenance. It calms the storms of the soul and teaches famine and fevers to laugh and sing; it is not a harsh or dejecting thing. (Anti-pattern: the scholastic notion that virtue is remote and severe, producing querulous, threatening images.)

rubrics_metrics.name: True virtue is accessible: easy, useful, and pleasurable in exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: “The height and value of true virtue consists in the facility, utility, and pleasure of its exercise; so far from difficulty, that boys, as well as men, and the innocent as well as the subtle, may make it their own; it is by order, and not by force, that it is to be acquired.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue should be taught as something naturally practicable and enjoyable, not as an austerely remote ideal. It moderates pleasures, makes them pure and lasting, and rules appetite by allowance rather than excessive prohibition (e.g., tempering the toper/glutton/lecher rather than denying all pleasure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach philosophy from childhood (early instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Since philosophy is that which instructs us to live, and that infancy has there its lessons as well as other ages, why is it not communicated to children betimes?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children have limited time (first 15–16 years) and can grasp practical philosophical lessons earlier than complicated formal learning; early education should focus on practical life-guidance rather than late, purely formal studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thorny subtleties and pedantic dialectics; prioritise plain practical discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: “Away with the thorny subtleties of dialectics; they are abuses, things by which our lives can never be amended: take the plain philosophical discourses… they are more easy to be understood than one of Boccaccio’s novels.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not load children with abstruse syllogisms or hair-splitting logic; teach the straightforward lessons about valour, temperance, magnanimity, and contempt of fear that are directly applicable to life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive bookishness and over-study; preserve balance
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would not have this pupil of ours imprisoned and made a slave to his book; nor would I have him given up to the morosity and melancholic humour of a sour ill-natured pedant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not subject children to extreme hours or solitary study (e.g., not fourteen or fifteen hours a day). Over-application to books can brutify and make one unfit for civil conversation and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gentle, attractive methods rather than rods and compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: “This method of education ought to be carried on with a severe sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants… Away with this violence! away with this compulsion!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tempt and allure children to learning by pleasant means (joyful classrooms, healthy food, games) rather than terrifying them with punishment and ferules. Quintilian cited: making chastisement savage breeds pernicious consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate physical exercise and bodily training with intellectual instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: “By which means our very exercises and recreations, running, wrestling, music, dancing, hunting, riding, and fencing, will prove to be a good part of our study. I would have his outward fashion and mien, and the disposition of his limbs, formed at the same time with his mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not train soul and body separately: provide regular bodily exercises and sports that contribute to character, vigor, and composure; make the pupil ‘a man’ not merely a soul or a body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form manners and deportment so conduct mirrors doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conduct of our lives is the true mirror of our doctrine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction must show itself in actions: prudence in exercises, sincerity and justice in deportment, grace and judgment in speaking, constancy in sickness, modesty in mirth, temperance in pleasures, order in domestic economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach adaptability: make the pupil fit for different fashions and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let a young man, in God’s name, be rendered fit for all nations and all companies… Let him be able to do everything, but love to do nothing but what is good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate flexibility of behavior (e.g., Alcibiades’ ability to conform to Persian pomp or Spartan austerity). This practical adaptability aids negotiation and social success; do not let scruples about trivial customs impede usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must teach moderation and how to lose goods without concern
rubrics_metrics.description: “She loves life, beauty, glory, and health; but her proper and peculiar office is to know how to regulate the use of all these good things, and how to lose them without concern.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach how to enjoy goods in measure and accept loss calmly; this is nobler than mere accumulation and prevents life from becoming turbulent and deformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning by practice and action rather than rote memory
rubrics_metrics.description: “The lad will not so much get his lesson by heart as he will practise it: he will repeat it in his actions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise lived exemplification over memorisation. Evaluate by observing behavior (temperance, modesty, constancy), not by rhetorical display alone. Action is the test of internalized doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not aim to produce grammarians/logicians when the goal is a gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now we who… do not here pretend to breed a grammarian or a logician, but a gentleman, let us leave them to abuse their leisure; our business lies elsewhere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid an education narrowly focused on technical linguistic or dialectical skill at the expense of broader moral, civic, and practical formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach languages early by immersion rather than protracted grammar drills
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne’s father employed a German who spoke only Latin to the child: by six years he “had learned to speak as pure Latin as my master himself, for I had no means of mixing it up with any other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early full-immersion (native-like household use) yields fluency with less pain than later tedious formal grammar; languages are valuable but must not be bought at the cost of the soul’s formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and speech should be natural, plain, and forceful rather than affected
rubrics_metrics.description: “The way of speaking that I love, is natural and plain, the same in writing as in speaking, and a sinewy and muscular way of expressing a man’s self, short and pithy, not so elegant and artificial as prompt and vehement… free from affectation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plainness, brevity, and force over elaborate ornament; affectation and exotic phrasing are puerile and scholastic. Encourage market-place perspicuity rather than artificial eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words must serve thought; invention and judgment matter more than ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: “Words are to serve, and to follow a man’s purpose… I would have things so excelling, and so wholly possessing the imagination of him that hears, that he should have something else to do, than to think of words.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate thought and invention first; when the idea is clear, words will follow. Eloquence that attracts attention to itself detracts from the subject it should advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not harden children to shame and chastisement; teach them sensitivity to proper shame
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you would have him apprehend shame and chastisement, do not harden him to them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose children to corrective sentiments without brutalisation; teach them modesty and the ability to accept chastisement without making them callous or debased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose children to varied conditions to correct singularities and hypersensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Inure him to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers that he ought to despise; wean him from all effeminacy and delicacy in clothes and lodging, eating and drinking… Young bodies are supple; one should, therefore, in that age bend and ply them to all fashions and customs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately accustom children to different diets, climates, noises, and hardships early so they do not grow delicate, squeamish, or peculiar in habit; prevention of odd aversions increases robustness and social competence.
